triage.name: Vitamin A deficiency
triage.reason: Night blindness and xerophthalmia with dietary history; exam findings are distinctive though the classic presentation is outside the US.

age.peak: bimodal: children under 5 in low-resource settings and adults with malabsorption or alcohol use disorder

demographics: Most common in low- and middle-income countries where vitamin A-rich foods are scarce
In the United States, seen mainly in the urban poor, recent immigrants, older adults, and people with alcohol use disorder or malabsorption
Children under 5 in low-resource settings are the group at highest risk worldwide

risk_factors.text: Diet lacking vitamin A-rich foods (liver, eggs, dairy, orange and dark green vegetables)
Fat malabsorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bariatric surgery)
Measles or other severe childhood infection
Pregnancy and lactation, especially with poor diet
Prematurity or very low birth weight
Low socioeconomic status or food insecurity

social_history: Recent immigration from a region with endemic vitamin A deficiency

chief_complaints.text: I can't see well at night or in dim light
My eyes feel dry and gritty
There are white foamy patches on the white of my eye
My child keeps getting infections and isn't growing well

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months as body stores are depleted
hpi.duration: Usually months of poor intake or malabsorption before symptoms appear
hpi.progression: Night blindness comes first, then dryness and surface changes of the eye; without treatment corneal ulceration and scarring can follow
hpi.quality: Poor vision in dim light, gritty dry eyes, sometimes a foreign-body sensation
hpi.severity: Mild at first, can become severe if the cornea is involved
hpi.timing: Worse at night and in dim light; eye dryness is constant
relieving: Artificial tears give only brief relief

associated_symptoms.text: White foamy patches on the conjunctiva
Frequent infections, especially respiratory and diarrheal
Eye pain and light sensitivity when the cornea is involved

pertinent_negatives: Eye redness and discharge suggesting infection

positives.text: White foamy patches on the conjunctiva

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children cannot report night blindness; they present with frequent infections, poor growth, and eye findings noticed by a caregiver.
Infants may show only failure to thrive, recurrent infection, and eye changes found on examination.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging or cataracts, and dietary deficiency is often unrecognized.
Increased vitamin A requirements can unmask deficiency, and night blindness is more prominent; severe deficiency raises maternal and infant risk.
Chronic liver disease impairs vitamin A storage and transport, so deficiency can occur even with adequate intake.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may squint or hesitate in dim light
general.moderate: Well-appearing but avoids dim light; dry, dull conjunctivae
general.severe: Ill-appearing, photophobic, keeps eyes closed, avoids light
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic, malnourished, corneal haze or perforation

findings.maneuver: Ask about vision in dim light and test dark adaptation or contrast sensitivity
findings.finding: Impaired vision in dim light or delayed dark adaptation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the bulbar conjunctiva in daylight
findings.finding: Dry, dull, wrinkled conjunctiva that loses its normal luster

findings.maneuver: Inspect the temporal conjunctiva with a penlight
findings.finding: Foamy, triangular white patches on the conjunctiva

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a penlight and fluorescein staining
findings.finding: Hazy, dry, lusterless cornea; punctate fluorescein uptake

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with fluorescein and a blue light
Inspect the cornea for softening or perforation
Inspect and palpate the skin of the arms, legs, and trunk
findings.finding: Dry, rough, scaly skin with follicular hyperkeratosis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the extensor surfaces of the arms and thighs
findings.finding: Rough, goosebump-like papules at hair follicles

findings.maneuver: Perform fundoscopy to examine the optic disc
Plot weight, length, and head circumference on a growth chart in children
findings.finding: Weight or length below the expected percentile for age

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and percuss the liver span
Palpate the cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes

labs.caveat: Low albumin reflects the underlying malnutrition or malabsorption rather than the vitamin A level itself.
Anemia is usually from coexisting iron, folate, or protein deficiency, not from vitamin A deficiency alone.
Microcytosis points to coexisting iron deficiency, which often accompanies poor vitamin A intake.
Inflammation lowers serum retinol and retinol-binding protein, so a low vitamin A level during infection can be misleading.

imaging.study: Ocular coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
imaging.preferred_when: When the fundus exam is limited or another macular cause of night blindness is suspected

findings.text: Thinning of the outer retinal layers with loss of the photoreceptor ellipsoid zone

imaging.study: Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment
imaging.preferred_when: Any patient with eye symptoms, to grade conjunctival and corneal changes

findings.text: Conjunctival xerosis with loss of luster and wrinkled surface
Bitot spots (foamy triangular patches on the conjunctiva)
Corneal xerosis with punctate fluorescein uptake
Usually normal; may show a focal infiltrate if a respiratory infection is present

initial.why: Looks for anemia and infection, which are common companions of vitamin A deficiency
Assesses albumin, liver enzymes, and calcium in a malnourished or malabsorbing patient

initial.test: Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment
initial.why: Grades conjunctival and corneal xerophthalmia and detects ulceration

initial.test: Visual acuity and dark adaptation testing
initial.why: Documents the functional visual deficit and response to treatment
Confirms the diagnosis when the history and eye findings are suggestive
Evaluates for pneumonia in a child with respiratory symptoms
initial.only_if: respiratory symptoms or fever suggest pneumonia

supporting.why: Helps interpret a low retinol level, since inflammation depresses retinol and retinol-binding protein
Rules out another vitamin deficiency that can cause visual or neurologic symptoms
Rules out coexisting folate deficiency in malnutrition or alcohol use disorder
Evaluates coexisting iron deficiency, which often accompanies poor diet
Screens for thyroid disease in a patient with nonspecific visual or systemic complaints
Screens for diabetes, which can cause visual symptoms and malabsorption-related deficiency

supporting.test: Ocular coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
supporting.why: Characterizes retinal changes when the fundus exam is limited or another macular cause is suspected
supporting.only_if: Characterizes retinal changes when the fundus exam is limited or another macular cause is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in nutritional eye disease
No role unless sepsis is suspected
Not needed unless pancreatic insufficiency is suspected as the cause of malabsorption
Not part of the vitamin A workup; order only if pregnancy status affects treatment or imaging decisions

decision_points: Measure serum retinol before starting supplementation when the diagnosis is uncertain
Interpret a low retinol level alongside CRP, because infection or inflammation lowers retinol
Treat severe eye findings (corneal ulcer, keratomalacia) as an emergency with immediate vitamin A and ophthalmology involvement
Look for and treat coexisting iron, folate, and protein malnutrition

differential.name: Vitamin D deficiency
differential.why_considered: Another fat-soluble vitamin deficiency that occurs in the same malnourished, malabsorbing, or housebound populations and can cause nonspecific weakness and bone pain.

history: Bone pain, muscle aches, or proximal weakness rather than night blindness
Little sun exposure, dark skin, or exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation
No gritty dry eyes or difficulty seeing in dim light
exam: Proximal muscle weakness, bone tenderness, or waddling gait
Normal conjunctivae and cornea without Bitot spots
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone
imaging: Rickets changes or osteopenia on x-ray when severe

differential.name: Retinitis pigmentosa
differential.why_considered: Inherited retinal degeneration that classically presents with night blindness and progressive peripheral vision loss, mimicking the earliest symptom of vitamin A deficiency.
differential.trigger: Night blindness with a family history of vision loss or no dietary or malabsorption risk factors

history: Family history of progressive night blindness or tunnel vision
Symptoms begin in childhood or adolescence and progress slowly over years
No poor diet, malabsorption, or alcohol use disorder
exam: Bone-spicule pigmentary changes in the peripheral retina
Constricted visual fields and reduced peripheral vision
Normal conjunctiva and cornea without xerosis
imaging: Electroretinogram shows reduced rod then cone responses
OCT shows outer retinal thinning in a pattern typical of rod-cone dystrophy

differential.name: Cataract
differential.why_considered: Clouding of the lens causes poor vision in dim light and glare, which older adults may describe as difficulty seeing at night.

history: Gradual blurring and glare rather than true night blindness
Difficulty with reading or driving at night but normal peripheral vision
No dietary deficiency or malabsorption
exam: Lens opacity seen on slit-lamp examination
Visual acuity improves with refraction or pinhole

differential.name: Open-angle glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Progressive optic neuropathy can cause loss of peripheral vision that patients notice first in dim light, overlapping with the visual complaints of vitamin A deficiency.
differential.trigger: Peripheral vision loss with an elevated intraocular pressure or cupped optic disc

history: Gradual loss of peripheral vision, often asymptomatic until advanced
Family history of glaucoma
No dry eyes, Bitot spots, or dietary risk factors
exam: Cupped optic disc with increased cup-to-disc ratio
imaging: OCT shows retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

differential.name: Congenital stationary night blindness
differential.why_considered: Inherited disorder of rod function that presents with lifelong night blindness and no eye surface changes, resembling the earliest stage of vitamin A deficiency.

history: Night blindness present since infancy or early childhood and stable over time
Family history of the same problem
No malnutrition or malabsorption
exam: Normal visual acuity in bright light
imaging: Electroretinogram shows a characteristic abnormal rod response with a normal or near-normal fundus

differential.name: Measles keratoconjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Measles is a precipitant of vitamin A deficiency and itself causes conjunctivitis and corneal involvement in children, so the two can coexist and be confused.
differential.trigger: Fever, rash, and conjunctivitis in an unvaccinated child

history: Fever, cough, coryza, and rash starting on the face and spreading downward
Recent exposure to measles or lack of vaccination
Acute onset over days rather than months
exam: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
Conjunctival injection and discharge rather than dry conjunctiva
labs: Serum retinol may also be low because measles depletes vitamin A

differential.name: Trachoma
differential.why_considered: Chronic Chlamydia trachomatis infection causes conjunctival scarring and corneal damage in the same low-resource settings where vitamin A deficiency is common.

history: Chronic red eyes with discharge and repeated infections
Flies around the face and poor hygiene
No true night blindness early on
exam: Follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva
labs: Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification testing from conjunctival swab

severity.mild: Night blindness and dry eyes only; no conjunctival or corneal surface changes on slit-lamp examination
severity.moderate: Conjunctival xerosis with or without Bitot spots; vision still preserved in bright light
severity.severe: Corneal xerosis with punctate fluorescein uptake; photophobia and eye pain; may have systemic signs of malnutrition
severity.critical: Corneal ulceration or keratomalacia with risk of perforation and permanent blindness; often with severe malnutrition or concurrent infection

red_flags.meaning: Sight-threatening ocular emergency; needs immediate vitamin A and urgent ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Severe malnutrition or failure to thrive
red_flags.meaning: Suggests advanced deficiency and increased risk of infection and death

red_flags.finding: Measles or another severe childhood infection
red_flags.meaning: Vitamin A deficiency worsens infection and infection worsens deficiency; treat both

red_flags.finding: Rapidly worsening vision or eye pain
red_flags.meaning: Possible corneal perforation or secondary infection; urgent evaluation required

complications.name: Corneal ulceration and scarring
clues: Corneal epithelial defect on fluorescein staining

complications.name: Keratomalacia with corneal perforation and blindness
Increased severity of infections (measles, diarrhea, respiratory)
Anemia and other coexisting nutritional deficiencies

special_populations.differences: Young children cannot report night blindness; they present with frequent infections, poor growth, and eye findings noticed by a caregiver. Deficiency is most severe and most common in children under 5 in low-resource settings.
Infants may show only failure to thrive, recurrent infection, and eye changes found on examination; maternal vitamin A status and breastfeeding matter.
Increased vitamin A requirements can unmask deficiency, and night blindness is more prominent. High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic, so supplementation must be dosed carefully in pregnancy.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging or cataracts, and dietary deficiency is often unrecognized; alcohol use disorder and malabsorption are common contributors.
Chronic liver disease impairs vitamin A storage and transport, so deficiency can occur even with adequate intake.

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble seeing at night or in dim light, like in a movie theater or when driving after dark?
key_questions.looking_for: Night blindness, the earliest and most consistent symptom

key_questions.question: When did this start, and has it gotten worse over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months, consistent with depletion of body stores

key_questions.question: Do your eyes feel dry, gritty, or like something is in them?
Have you or anyone noticed white foamy patches on the white of your eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Bitot spots, a hallmark of xerophthalmia

key_questions.question: What did you eat over the past few weeks? Do you eat liver, eggs, dairy, or orange and dark green vegetables?
key_questions.looking_for: A diet lacking vitamin A-rich foods

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea, greasy stools, or trouble gaining weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Fat malabsorption from celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency, or cholestasis

key_questions.question: Have you had stomach or intestinal surgery, including weight-loss surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Bariatric surgery or bowel resection causing malabsorption

key_questions.question: Do you have any liver disease, or have you been told your liver tests were abnormal?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic liver disease impairing vitamin A storage and transport

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
key_questions.looking_for: Alcohol use disorder, a common cause in US adults

key_questions.question: Are you taking any weight-loss medications or cholesterol-lowering powders?
key_questions.looking_for: Orlistat, cholestyramine, colestipol, or colesevelam, which impair fat and vitamin A absorption

key_questions.question: Has your child been getting frequent infections, especially diarrhea or pneumonia, or not growing well?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent infection and failure to thrive in children

key_questions.question: Has there been a recent measles illness or exposure?
key_questions.looking_for: Measles, which both precipitates and worsens vitamin A deficiency

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of night blindness or progressive vision loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited retinal dystrophy such as retinitis pigmentosa

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant or breastfeeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Increased vitamin A requirements and the need for careful dosing because high-dose vitamin A is teratogenic

key_questions.question: Any eye pain, light sensitivity, or sudden change in vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Corneal involvement or keratomalacia, a sight-threatening emergency

reasoning_points: Night blindness is the earliest and most consistent symptom, followed by dryness and surface changes of the eye
A diet lacking vitamin A-rich foods, or a condition causing fat malabsorption, explains the deficiency
Risk factors include alcohol use disorder, chronic liver disease, bariatric surgery, and malabsorption syndromes
Examination shows conjunctival xerosis, Bitot spots, and in severe cases corneal xerosis, ulceration, or keratomalacia
The eye findings are bilateral and occur without redness or discharge, which argues against infection
Serum retinol is low, but must be interpreted alongside CRP because inflammation lowers retinol
Coexisting iron, folate, and protein malnutrition should be looked for and treated
Corneal ulceration or keratomalacia is an emergency requiring immediate vitamin A and ophthalmology involvement

easy: Child in a low-resource setting with classic night blindness and Bitot spots
Clear dietary history of little or no vitamin A-rich food
Bilateral dry eyes without redness or discharge
Low serum retinol confirms the diagnosis
medium: Adult with alcohol use disorder and poor diet presenting with night blindness
Patient with celiac disease or cystic fibrosis and chronic malabsorption
Older adult whose visual symptoms are attributed to aging or cataracts
Coexisting iron or folate deficiency masking the picture
hard: Infant who cannot report night blindness and presents only with failure to thrive and recurrent infection
Pregnant patient with increased requirements and prominent night blindness but no Bitot spots
Patient with chronic liver disease and adequate intake but impaired storage and transport
Corneal ulcer or keratomalacia presenting as an eye emergency without a known deficiency history
